name: The goal: specifying a construct before anything exists to build it from
description: state what must be true of a construct — its devices, the ordered slots each is made of, and the rules that hold across them — then enumerate every design that satisfies it and see why the rest do not. The Eugene-derived constraint layer and the goal document that feeds it
phrases: what do I want to build
write a goal for a construct
constrain which parts may be combined
enumerate the designs that satisfy my constraints
declare a part type and its properties
operon structure before I know what plasmids exist

data.scope: Phase 1a of experimental planning: what must be true of the construct, written as a document and checked by code. Devices, slots, part types and properties, and the rules that constrain how they compose. It is NOT the search for what exists — a goal names no plasmid and no box, and whether the parts can be had is phase 1b. It is NOT the cloning design: how the construct gets ASSEMBLED is a construction file and belongs to phase 2. It is NOT a judge of whether a design is a good idea — validation here is structural, and a goal that passes may still be a bad experiment.
invariants: AN UNDECLARED PROPERTY IS AN ERROR, NOT AN EXTRA FIELD. `.Strenght(0.7)` is silently absent, every rule written against it is then vacuously true, and the design passes constraints nobody applied. A rule that cannot fail is the defect this layer exists to prevent, so `eugene.makepart` throws rather than carrying the value.

AN UNKNOWN RULE OPERATOR THROWS RATHER THAN BEING SKIPPED. The same failure one layer up: a constraint quietly dropped from a goal file becomes a check that was never applied. A goal with a typo in an operator does not load.

A REJECTED DESIGN COMES BACK WITH THE CLAUSE THAT KILLED IT, and a part type nothing can fill is NAMED rather than yielding an empty result. 'Nothing satisfies these rules' and 'nothing of that type is in the library' want different actions from a person — loosen a constraint, or go and find a part.

A CAPPED ENUMERATION SAYS IT WAS CAPPED. The product of a few open slots over a real parts library is large, so the search is bounded; a bounded search reporting itself as complete would be a wrong answer wearing a right one's clothes.

A PART WITH NO SEQUENCE IS NAMED, NOT SKIPPED. Specs are routinely written before every part has one — that is what phase 1a is for — and a concatenation that omitted them would return a shorter construct that looks finished.

THE VOCABULARY IS DERIVED FROM EUGENE AND SAYS SO. Bilitchenko, Liu, Cheung, Weeding, Xia, Leguia, Anderson, Densmore, PLoS ONE 6(4):e18882, 2011. The operators that paper demonstrates keep their names; the ones it does not are marked EXTENSION in the code, so nobody later cites this toolkit as evidence that Eugene had them.

branches.name: write
branches.what: the goal document — its shape, and what `intent` is for

branches.name: validate
branches.what: is it well formed — every problem at once, not the first. `goal.validategoal`

branches.name: enumerate
branches.what: every design the goal allows and every one it does not, with reasons. `goal.goaltospec` then `eugene.enumeratedesigns`

branches.name: parts
branches.what: declaring part types and instantiating parts, checked. `eugene.defineparttype`, `eugene.makepart`

branches.name: out
branches.what: the DNA a device specifies, and a line a person can choose from. `eugene.devicesequence`, `eugene.describedevice`

notes: WRITTEN 2026-11-04 alongside the code it documents. The split between a goal as DATA and the rules as COMPILED PREDICATES is the load-bearing decision: a goal expressed as code could only be reviewed by running it, and the whole reason this phase exists is that a design has to be reviewable without trusting whoever produced it.
